paper.title_en: EP241206a: A Sub-kilosecond X-Ray Flare Possibly from an Active Galactic Nucleus with a Flux Increase over 3 Orders of Magnitude
paper.abstract_en: EP241206a is a fast X-ray transient detected with the Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) on board the Einstein Probe. The event exhibited a single-peaked soft X-ray flare with a duration of ∼500 s and a peak flux of 1.0 × 10$^{−9}$ erg s$^{−1}$cm$^{−2}$ in 0.5-4 keV, spatially coincident with a spectroscopically confirmed active galactic nucleus (AGN) at z = 0.62. Follow-up and archival observations revealed persistent X-ray emission at a level of ∼5 × 10$^{−13}$ erg s$^{−1}$cm$^{−2}$, corresponding to L$_{2−10 keV}$ ≃ 2.3 × 10$^{44}$ erg s$^{−1}$ if associated with the AGN; the WXT flare reached an estimated peak isotropic-equivalent rest-frame 2-10 keV luminosity of ∼1.4 × 10$^{48}$ erg s$^{−1}$, implying a peak-to-persistent luminosity contrast of over 3 orders of magnitude. Optical spectroscopy detected broad Mg ii and Hβ emission lines, suggesting a black hole mass of ∼3.8 × 10$^{7}$M$_{⊙}$ and Eddington ratios of 0.8 at the persistent state versus an apparent peak ratio of ∼4.6 × 10$^{3}$ during the flare. The extremely short duration and high apparent peak luminosity favor a jet origin, likely due to magnetic reconnection in the inner regions of a relativistic jet. Alternative scenarios include a jet-in-the-jet or a gamma-ray burst occurring within the AGN disk. However, the physical association between the transient and the AGN is not firmly established; for the radio-loud and X-ray-detected AGN counterpart class, the trial-corrected chance probability is 4.9 × 10$^{−3}$. EP241206a may represent an example of a broader population of unidentified fast X-ray transients detected with WXT.
